st-augustine.intro: St. Augustine's most famous tree stands in a hotel parking lot on San Marco Avenue, behind a black iron railing, with a palm growing out of its crown. The marker beside the Old Senator says the live oak is well over 600 years old and ties it to Ponce de León's landing in 1513, about 600 feet from the Fountain of Youth. Nobody has dated it, so take the number as legend. The tree itself is real, big and hung with Spanish moss, and the sightseeing trolleys pass it.
st-augustine.meta_description: The Old Senator, St. Augustine's live oak on San Marco Avenue, reputed at over 600 years: where it stands, what its marker claims and what is known.
st-augustine.question_meta: Is the Old Senator in St. Augustine really 600 years old? What the claim rests on, and how to see the live oak on San Marco Avenue.
st-augustine.question_answer: Nobody knows, and the number is best read as legend. The Old Senator's marker and Visit St. Augustine say the live oak is more than 600 years old, and a tourism blog says about 650, but none of them gives a dating method and no ring count has been published. The tree itself stands in the courtyard lot of the Villa 1565 hotel at 137 San Marco Avenue, a few blocks north of the Historic District, fenced and marked, and recent photographs show it alive.
st-augustine.question_context: The 600 years arrive with a story attached. The marker beside the trunk links the tree to Ponce de León's landing in 1513 and places it about 600 feet from the Fountain of Youth, and local lore credits its long life to that spring. Another piece of lore says couples who kiss beneath it stay together. Neither is history, and the sizes in circulation are no better: one account gives a height of 56 feet, another gives figures with no units, and they cannot be reconciled. What can be checked is simpler. It is a large southern live oak hung with Spanish moss, a sabal palm grows from its crown, and visitors have photographed it at this spot since at least 2010. The land belongs to the hotel, but the tree is shown to visitors, so look from the lot and keep out of the guest areas. There is no fee and no published opening time. The Old Town Trolley and the Red Train both pass, a Red Train bench stands beside the railing, and the Plaza de la Constitución is a few blocks south on foot.

faq.q: Where is the Old Senator tree in St. Augustine?
faq.a: In the courtyard and parking lot of the Villa 1565 hotel at 137 San Marco Avenue, a few blocks north of the Historic District. The trunk is fenced with a black iron railing and has a marker beside it.

faq.q: Can you visit the Old Senator?
faq.a: Yes. It stands on private hotel land, but the tree is shown to visitors and there is no fee. View it from the lot and stay out of the guest areas.

faq.q: Is it true that couples who kiss under the Old Senator stay together?
faq.a: That is local lore, along with the idea that the nearby Fountain of Youth keeps the tree alive. Nobody has documented either. The tree's age of more than 600 years is a claim of the same kind, repeated without a dating method.

tallahassee.intro: Tallahassee's great oak grows on the grounds of a small cottage on High Road. When public radio station WFSU measured the Lichgate Oak in 2019, the trunk was about 215 centimetres across, close to seven metres round, and a forester's calculation from that put it at about 175 years. A local tree service says several hundred. It is the city's oak to see now that the May Oak, its other famous tree, collapsed in 1986. The grounds have been on the National Register of Historic Places since 2006 and are open to the public.
tallahassee.meta_description: The Lichgate Oak on High Road, Tallahassee: a live oak about seven metres round, how old it is thought to be, and how to visit the grounds.
tallahassee.question_meta: How old is the Lichgate Oak in Tallahassee? About 175 years by a forester's calculation, several hundred by another account. How it was worked out.
tallahassee.question_answer: About 175 years, by the only estimate that shows its working. In 2019 the public radio station WFSU measured the trunk at about 84.7 inches across, roughly 215 centimetres, and a forester calculated an age of 172 years from it, rounded to 175. A local tree service calls the oak several hundred years old but gives no basis. Nobody has counted its rings, so the fair answer is from about 175 years upward.
tallahassee.question_context: A growth calculation works an age out from the size of the trunk, which is why it gives a single number, and why the forester rounded 172 to 175 rather than pretend to the year. Live oaks are hard to date that way, because they grow fast when young and slow down unpredictably later, so the result is a guide rather than a count. The other figure in circulation, several hundred years, comes from a local tree service and has no basis given. What is not in doubt is the size. A trunk about 215 centimetres across works out at close to seven metres round, and the crown spreads wide enough that a photograph from beneath shows little else. The oak stands on the grounds of Lichgate on High Road, a cottage and garden in north Tallahassee. The land was bought in 1955, a group took over its care after its owner died in 1995, and the property went on the National Register in 2006. A short wooded path leads from a small parking lot on the property. Listings give the hours as dawn to dusk with no fee, but check Lichgate's own website first.

faq.q: Can you visit the Lichgate Oak?
faq.a: Yes. The grounds of Lichgate on High Road are open to the public, reached by a short wooded path from a small parking lot. Listings give dawn to dusk with no admission fee; check Lichgate's own website before you go.

faq.q: How big is the Lichgate Oak?
faq.a: WFSU measured the trunk in 2019 at about 84.7 inches across, roughly 215 centimetres, which is close to seven metres around. The crown spreads wide enough to fill the view from underneath.

faq.q: What happened to Tallahassee's May Oak?
faq.a: It collapsed in 1986. Tallahassee's other famous oaks are gone too, which leaves the Lichgate Oak as the one to visit.

tampa.intro: Tampa's best-known oak comes with a plaque that admits it is telling a story. The DeSoto Oak in Plant Park, beside Plant Hall on the University of Tampa campus, carries a tablet saying that tradition places a meeting between De Soto and native people under its branches. Early residents remembered it standing before the Tampa Bay Hotel opened in 1891. Nobody has published an age or a size, but the park is free, open ground on the Hillsborough River, a short walk from the Riverwalk.
tampa.meta_description: The DeSoto Oak in Plant Park, Tampa: the live oak where tradition says De Soto met native people, what is known, and how to find its plaque.
tampa.question_meta: Did De Soto really meet anyone under Tampa's DeSoto Oak? What the plaque says, what is known about the tree, and where it stands.
tampa.question_answer: Nobody can show that he did, and the plaque does not claim it. The tablet at the foot of the DeSoto Oak in Plant Park, put up by the De Soto Chapter of the Daughters of the American Revolution, marks the tree under which tradition says De Soto parlayed with the Indians. That is a tradition, not a record. What the Henry B. Plant Museum does record is that early Tampa residents said the oak was standing before the Tampa Bay Hotel was built, and the hotel opened in 1891.
tampa.question_context: That recollection is the only age anyone has offered for the DeSoto Oak, and it only says older than 1891, if the memory is right. There is no ring count, girth, height or register entry, so the honest age is unknown, and anyone who has measured the tree can tell us. Plant Park itself is the open ground beside Plant Hall on the University of Tampa campus, running down to the Hillsborough River. It holds many planted oaks and a palm walk from the 1890s, so the plaque stone at its foot is what tells this tree from the others. Two other oaks on the campus were moved there in 2000, and a large transplanted oak won a university award in 2012. Neither is this one. Postcards from the early twentieth century show a large live oak in the grounds, though nobody has checked that it is this trunk. No storm damage to it was reported after Hurricane Milton in 2024. Entry is free from the pavement on University Drive, and the TECO Line Streetcar and the Riverwalk are about ten minutes away on foot.

faq.q: Where is the DeSoto Oak in Tampa?
faq.a: In Plant Park, on University Drive beside Plant Hall on the University of Tampa campus, near the Hillsborough River. Look for the DAR plaque on a stone at its foot.

faq.q: How old is the DeSoto Oak?
faq.a: Nobody has published an age. Early Tampa residents remembered it standing before the Tampa Bay Hotel opened in 1891, which is local memory rather than a measurement.

faq.q: Is Plant Park free to visit?
faq.a: Yes. It is open ground beside Plant Hall, walk-up from the pavement, about ten minutes on foot from the TECO Line Streetcar and the Riverwalk.

safety-harbor.intro: Safety Harbor built a park around one tree and, in March 2024, asked its voters to protect both in perpetuity. The Baranoff Oak stands in the middle of downtown, a live oak with a trunk nearly 20 feet round, said to be between 300 and 500 years old and thought to be the oldest tree in Pinellas County. It was the Safety Harbor Oak until 2004, when it became the centrepiece of the park that now carries its name. Entry is free.
safety-harbor.meta_description: The Baranoff Oak in Safety Harbor, Florida: a live oak said to be 300 to 500 years old, the town's vote to protect it, and how to get there from Tampa.
safety-harbor.question_meta: How old is the Baranoff Oak in Safety Harbor? Said to be 300 to 500 years, with no ring count. What is known, and how to reach it from Tampa.
safety-harbor.question_answer: Somewhere between 300 and 500 years, by the estimate WUSF and a visitors' waymark both repeat, and nobody has counted its rings. WUSF, Tampa Bay's public radio station, adds that it is thought to be the oldest tree in Pinellas County. The trunk is nearly 20 feet around, about six metres, by the waymark's figure. It stands at the centre of Baranoff Park in downtown Safety Harbor, free and open.
safety-harbor.question_context: A range that wide is the honest shape of a live oak's age. The species grows fast when young and slows unpredictably, and big ones are rarely cored, so most ages are estimates handed from one account to the next. The Baranoff Oak's own history is better documented than its birth. It was known as the Safety Harbor Oak until 2004, when it became the centrepiece of a new pocket park and took its present name. Being on show has not always helped it. The Tampa Bay Times once reported that an effort to showcase the tree harmed it and that arborists worked to restore it, and photographs from October 2026 show it alive, its branches spreading over the park. In March 2024 WUSF reported that voters were being asked to protect the park and the tree in perpetuity. Safety Harbor is a town of its own in Pinellas County, about 20 miles west of downtown Tampa and roughly half an hour by car. PSTA buses reach it only with a change, so for most visitors it is a short drive rather than a ride.

faq.q: Is the Baranoff Oak the oldest tree in Pinellas County?
faq.a: It is thought to be, WUSF reported in 2024. That is a belief rather than a measured record, since nobody has counted its rings, and its age is given as 300 to 500 years.

faq.q: How do you get to the Baranoff Oak from Tampa?
faq.a: By car it is about 20 miles west of downtown Tampa, roughly half an hour. PSTA buses reach Safety Harbor only with a change. The oak is in Baranoff Park in the middle of downtown.

faq.q: Why is it called the Baranoff Oak?
faq.a: It took the name in 2004, when it became the centrepiece of Baranoff Park. Before that it was simply the Safety Harbor Oak.

orlando.intro: Orlando keeps more than 100,000 trees and names one of them its oldest, a live oak with a park of its own on Thornton Avenue, struck by lightning at least three times in the 1970s. The city puts the Big Tree at likely 350 to 400 years. In Loch Haven Park, The Mayor has broken limbs twice and still lets the rest hang to the ground. And in Thornton Park, near Lake Eola, the oak of Constitution Green was saved in 2015 when the land it stands on came up for sale.
orlando.meta_description: Three live oaks in Orlando: the Big Tree, the city's oldest at 350 to 400 years, The Mayor in Loch Haven Park, and the oak of Constitution Green.
orlando.question_meta: Orlando's oldest tree is the Big Tree, a live oak put at 350 to 400 years in its own park on Thornton Avenue. Where it stands, and two more oaks.
orlando.question_answer: The oldest tree in Orlando is the live oak in Big Tree Park on North Thornton Avenue, named the oldest of the city's more than 100,000 maintained trees by its parks department. The City of Orlando says it is likely between 350 and 400 years old, and a USA Today network report says more than 400. Neither figure comes from a ring count. Do not confuse it with Big Tree Park in Longwood, north of the city, whose Senator fell in 2012.
orlando.question_context: All three of Orlando's oaks here are on the city's own Significant Trees list, and all three ages are estimates. The Big Tree's 350 to 400 years is the city's figure. Its trunk is reported as thick as 8 feet, without saying whether across or around, and its limbs reach out more than 30 feet each side. The city put up a placard there in the 1920s and bought the land about 30 years later, and recently a Michigan nonprofit, the Archangel Ancient Tree Archive, took samples to clone it. The Mayor, in Loch Haven Park beside the Mennello Museum, is put at over 200 years by the city and more than 300 by a newspaper feature. It broke limbs in 1998 and 2008, and its information display claims it had reached a third of its height when the Constitution was ratified. The oak at Constitution Green in Thornton Park is the youngest, probably 125 to 175 years by the city's reckoning, and has a crown shaped by a tree that once stood opposite. All three are free to visit.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Orlando?
faq.a: The live oak in Big Tree Park on North Thornton Avenue. The city says it is likely 350 to 400 years old and calls it the oldest tree in Orlando; a newspaper report says more than 400. Neither comes from a ring count.

faq.q: Is Big Tree Park in Orlando the same as the one in Longwood?
faq.a: No. Orlando's Big Tree Park is a small city park on Thornton Avenue north of downtown. The Big Tree Park in Longwood is a different place, where the Senator fell in 2012 and Lady Liberty still stands.

faq.q: How was the Constitution Green oak saved?
faq.a: In 2015 the land it stands on was leased from a private family who wanted to sell. A public campaign followed, and the city announced it would save both the tree and the green.

faq.q: Where is The Mayor in Orlando?
faq.a: In Loch Haven Park, on the lawn beside the Mennello Museum of American Art, north of downtown. An information display stands near the tree, and entry to the park is free.

jacksonville.intro: Jacksonville once had five great oaks, by the county's urban forestry count, and two are left. The Treaty Oak on the Southbank is named after a treaty that was never signed, a story a newspaper reporter told in the 1930s to save it from developers. Its crown spreads about 145 feet over a free city park. Across the river in Riverside, the Cummer Oak is the reason a museum built its galleries on pilings, and the gardens around it were laid out in its shade.
jacksonville.meta_description: Jacksonville's two surviving great oaks: the Treaty Oak in Jessie Ball duPont Park, named for a treaty never signed, and the Cummer Oak in Riverside.
jacksonville.question_meta: Was a treaty really signed under Jacksonville's Treaty Oak? No. Where the name came from, how old the oak is, and the city's other great oak.
jacksonville.question_answer: No. In the 1930s a Florida Times-Union reporter wrote that a treaty with native people had been signed beneath the oak, to save it from developers, and later sources describe that story as invented. The name stuck. Before it the tree was called the Giant Oak. It stands in Jessie Ball duPont Park on the Southbank, about 70 feet tall with a trunk more than 25 feet round, and its age is put at about 250 years by the city, under 200 by a visitors' waymark.
jacksonville.question_context: The invented treaty worked. From 1907 the land around the oak had been the Dixieland Amusement Park, with the tree strung with lights. In about 1934 the Garden Club and a philanthropist bought the ground, her trust gave it to the city in 1964 on condition that it stay a park whose purpose includes preserving the oak, and the park has carried her name since 1971. Cables and lightning protection went in during 1995, and a boardwalk built in 1994 keeps feet off the roots. Nobody has cored it, and in 2006 arborists said it could live another 400 years. The county's urban forestry office lists four other great oaks that once stood in Jacksonville, of which only the Cummer Oak survives. That one grows at the Cummer Museum of Art & Gardens in Riverside, 80 feet tall with a trunk 21 feet round, and the gardens put it at 175 to 200 years. It was already a big tree when the Cummer family arrived in the late 1890s. Seeing it means a paid museum visit; the Treaty Oak's park is free.

faq.q: How old is the Treaty Oak in Jacksonville?
faq.a: Estimates differ. The city and Visit Jacksonville give about 250 years, and a visitors' waymark says under 200. Nobody has cored it, so neither is a measurement.

faq.q: Is the Treaty Oak free to visit?
faq.a: Yes. It stands in Jessie Ball duPont Park, a free city park on the Southbank of the St. Johns River, with a boardwalk running under the canopy.

faq.q: Can you see the Cummer Oak without paying?
faq.a: No. It stands in the Italian Garden at the Cummer Museum of Art & Gardens in Riverside, which is part of the paid museum visit during museum hours. Check the museum's website for times and prices.

la-crosse-florida.intro: Near LaCrosse, about 19 km north-west of Gainesville, Alachua County keeps ten acres of mown lawn for a single live oak. The Cellon Oak is 91 feet tall with a trunk 390 inches round, about 9.9 metres, and a crown spreading 171 feet, by the state champion tree register's 2018 measurement. It is listed as Florida's co-champion live oak and is put at more than 200 years. In 2025 the county closed the park for two days to fit new lightning protection. You need a car to get there.
la-crosse-florida.meta_description: The Cellon Oak near LaCrosse, Florida: a co-champion live oak 91 feet tall in its own county park, about 19 km north-west of Gainesville.
la-crosse-florida.question_meta: Is the Cellon Oak still Florida's champion live oak? What the register says, what changed in 2022, and how to reach it from Gainesville.
la-crosse-florida.question_answer: Not on its own. The Florida Forest Service register lists the Cellon Oak as Florida's co-champion live oak, measured in 2018 at 390 inches round, 91 feet tall and with a crown of 171 feet. In October 2022, WUFT reported, the title passed to a live oak on private land elsewhere in Alachua with a thicker trunk, 36.5 feet round. The Cellon Oak is still about 13 feet the taller of the two.
la-crosse-florida.question_context: The tree that took the title in 2022 is 78 feet tall with a crown of 180 feet and stands on private land. The Cellon Oak stands in a county park, bought by Alachua County in 1989 and free to enter. The park is little more than the tree. A ten-acre mown lawn surrounds it, with two picnic tables and a grill and no restrooms. Its age is an estimate. A 2019 WUFT caption put its planting at about 1832, a local television station says more than 200 years, and nobody has cored it. Lightning is the county's main worry, and in April 2025 it shut the park for two days to install a new protection system. You will see the name spelled Ceylon in some older reports; Cellon is the park's own spelling. The park lies near LaCrosse, about 19 km north-west of central Gainesville. We found no public transport, so plan on a car, and confirm the hours before you go.

faq.q: How far is the Cellon Oak from Gainesville?
faq.a: About 19 km north-west of central Gainesville and the University of Florida, near LaCrosse. No public transport goes there that we could find, so it is a drive.

faq.q: How big is the Cellon Oak?
faq.a: The state champion tree register measured it in 2018 at 390 inches round, about 9.9 metres, 91 feet tall, with a crown spreading 171 feet.

faq.q: Is it Cellon Oak or Ceylon Oak?
faq.a: Both spellings appear. Older press reports and a university fact sheet write Ceylon; the register and the park itself use Cellon.

austin.intro: Twelve trees, and three of them are groves, because that is how Austin's oldest survived. A live oak downtown lived through a deliberate poisoning in 1989. A block away is the grove the city was auctioned beneath in 1839. On the university campus stand the Battle Oaks and a mesquite left from the days when thousands grew here. A state co-champion oak grew up wild on Waller Creek, and the 2008 Tree of the Year grows behind a supermarket. Sunset Valley holds the national champion Bigelow oak, and a bald cypress written about in 1716 is worth the drive.
austin.meta_description: Twelve remarkable trees in Austin: the Treaty Oak that survived poisoning, a state champion Durand oak, and a cypress older than Texas.
austin.question_meta: Austin's oldest tree is Old Baldy, a bald cypress on Onion Creek past 500 years old. Where it stands, and eleven more worth the walk.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Austin?
faq.a: Old Baldy, a bald cypress on Onion Creek in McKinney Falls State Park. Texas Parks and Wildlife calls it the oldest bald cypress on public land in Texas and dates it past five hundred years. A Franciscan priest wrote about it in 1716. The Treaty Oak downtown is close behind at around five hundred.

faq.q: Can you still visit the Treaty Oak after the poisoning?
faq.a: Yes. It stands in its own small park on Baylor Street, free and open, a few minutes west of the 6th Street bars. Roughly two thirds of the tree died after it was poisoned in 1989 and more than half the crown had to be cut away, so what you see is lopsided rather than the wide dome in the old photographs. It set acorns again in 1997 and has gone on doing so.

faq.q: Why are three of the twelve listed as groves rather than single trees?
faq.a: Because that is what they are, and each one is the destination rather than any single trunk in it. The Auction Oaks, the Battle Oaks and the Seiders Oaks are all named, compact stands that people go to as a group, which is how the sources treat them and how the plaques read.

faq.q: Which live oak are these, exactly?
faq.a: For the Battle Oaks the university says Texas live oak, Quercus fusiformis, and the Treaty Oak is recorded as the same. For the Auction Oaks and the Seiders Oaks nobody we can find has settled it. Central Texas has two live oaks that look much alike and the sources simply say live oak. If you know which, tell us and we will fix it.

faq.q: Are these all the historic trees in Austin?
faq.a: No. The Texas A&M Forest Service register lists ten around the city, and several of them no longer stand. A bastard oak on the Waller Creek greenbelt and a Himalayan cedar on the university campus, both once flagged here as needing a second source, are now on this page as the Durand Oak of Sir Swante Palm Park and the Littlefield Cedar.

faq.q: Where is the Central Market oak?
faq.a: In Central Park, behind the Central Market store on North Lamar Boulevard. Walk out the back of the store and follow the gravel path along the pond; the 2008 Tree of the Year sign stands by the tree. It is free, and buses stop on North Lamar about five minutes away.

houston.intro: Houston does not do walks, and neither does this page. The city sprawls across seventeen hundred square kilometres and its oldest trees are scattered accordingly: a live oak with a forty metre crown in Spring Branch, the tallest winged elm in Texas, a pecan with a footpath named after it, a live oak in Klein a gas station nearly took down, a yaupon in a museum garden, a wide oak in Bellaire, two old live oaks downtown, and the post oaks at a cemetery gate in Montrose that a hurricane thinned in 2024. Twelve trees, each worth the trip.
houston.meta_description: Twelve remarkable trees around Houston: a live oak with a 40 metre crown, the tallest winged elm in Texas, and two old live oaks downtown.
houston.question_meta: Houston's oldest tree is the Kissing Tree at Klein, a live oak that marks an 1848 homestead. Where it stands, and eleven more worth the trip.

goliad.intro: Goliad keeps three old trees within a short drive of each other. On the north lawn of the courthouse, the Cart War Oak shaded court sessions from 1846 to 1870 and, by the state marker's account as quoted, was used for hangings, among them during the Cart War of 1857. A block west, the Baptist Oak marks where twelve Baptists met in May 1849, and cars have hit it many times since. South of town at Mission Espíritu Santo, an anaqua put at about two centuries was dug up in the 1930s and moved to save it.
goliad.meta_description: Three old trees in Goliad, Texas: the Cart War Oak on the courthouse lawn, the Baptist Oak and the anaqua moved to save it at Mission Espíritu Santo.
goliad.question_meta: Goliad's oldest dated tree is the anaqua at Mission Espíritu Santo, put at about two centuries. Where it stands, and two old oaks in town.
goliad.question_answer: No tree in Goliad has been measured or ring-counted, so the oldest is a matter of estimates. The highest published one belongs to the anaqua at Mission Espíritu Santo, in Goliad State Park, which the Texas A&M Forest Service calls more than two centuries old and Wikipedia nearly two. The Baptist Oak in town is credited with more than 160 years. The Cart War Oak on the courthouse lawn has no published age, though the state marker's account, as quoted, has court meeting under it from 1846.
goliad.question_context: The anaqua is the odd one out, a south Texas native rather than an oak, and the only one of the three that has moved. In the 1930s, when the Civilian Conservation Corps was rebuilding the mission, it stood where the patio is now, and the architect in charge had it dug up with a root ball eighteen feet across and replanted away from the building. Texas Parks and Wildlife's magazine says it took root among the ruins after the Spanish built the mission in 1749, so it is younger than the mission. The park charges a day-use fee and lies about 3 km south of town by car. The two oaks are in town, about 150 metres apart and free to see. The Cart War Oak stands on the courthouse lawn, in front of a Second Empire courthouse of 1894, and was photographed alive in 2015. The Baptist Oak stands on the edge of South Chilton Street beside a 1999 state marker. A 2011 accident cost it a major limb, and nobody has shown that it is the same oak the Baptists met under in 1849.

faq.q: Where is the Goliad Hanging Tree?
faq.a: On the north lawn of the Goliad County Courthouse, on the town square, beside a state historical marker.

faq.q: Can I visit the Cart War Oak?
faq.a: Yes. The courthouse lawn is open ground on the town square, with no ticket to buy.

faq.q: Is the Baptist Oak the tree the first Baptists met under in 1849?
faq.a: The state marker and the Texas A&M Forest Service tie the two together, but nobody has measured the tree or counted its rings. The Forest Service says it has stood for more than 160 years.

faq.q: Do you have to pay to see the Goliad anaqua?
faq.a: Yes. It stands in front of the museum at Mission Espíritu Santo, inside Goliad State Park and Historic Site, which charges a day-use fee, listed at $4 a person in November 2026.
